label: thm:main-graphs
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main-graphs}Let $H$ be a strictly 2-balanced graph which is not the 2-edge path\footnote{The 2-edge path anyway does not satisfy our definition of ``strictly 2-balanced'', but we emphasise this point since there is some inconsistency in the literature on this matter (some authors consider the 2-edge path to be strictly 2-balanced).}, and let $\varepsilon,\delta>0$. Let $X_H(G)$ be the number of copies of $H$ in a graph $G$, and let $X_H(\vec q)$ be the expected value of $X_H(G)$ for $G\sim \mathbb G(n,\vec q)$. Then, the following hold for sufficiently large $n$. 
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Let $p\in [\delta n^{-1/d_2(H)},\delta^{-1}n^{-1/d_2(H)}]$, let $G\sim \mathbb G(n,p)$, and let $0\le L\le (1-\delta)\mathbb EX_H(G)$. Then
\[
\log \mathbb P[X_H(G)\le L]=-\min_{\vec{q}\in \mathcal Q}\Big(\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,p)+\Phi_L(X_H(\vec q))\Big)\pm \varepsilon p\binom n2,
\]
where $\mathcal Q=[0,p]^{K_n}$ is the set of edge-weightings of $K_n$ with weights in the range $[0,p]$.
\item Let $m\in [\delta n^{2-1/d_2(H)},\delta^{-1}n^{2-1/d_2(H)}]$, let $G\sim \mathbb G(n,m)$, and let $0\le L\le (1-\delta)\mathbb EX_H(G)$. Then
\[
\log \mathbb P[X_H(G)\le L]=-\min_{\vec{q}\in \mathcal Q_{m}}\Big(\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,m/{\textstyle{\binom n2}})+\Phi_L(X_H(\vec q))\Big)\pm \varepsilon m,
\]
where $\mathcal Q_m\subseteq[0,1]^{K_n}$ is the set of edge-weightings of $K_n$ whose weights sum to exactly $m$.
    \end{enumerate}

label: cor:main-graphs
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:main-graphs}Fix a strictly 2-balanced graph $H$ which is not the 2-edge path, and fix $c> 0$ and $z\in [0,1)$. Let $\operatorname{Aut}(H)$ be the automorphism group of $H$, let $t_H(W)=\int_0^1\dots \int_0^1\prod_{ij\in H}W(x_i,x_j)\operatorname dx_1\dots\operatorname d x_{v(H)}$ be the homomorphism density of $H$ in $W$ and let 
    \[\psi_z(t)=\begin{cases}
        t-z+z\log(z/t)&\text{if }t> z,\\
        0&\text{if }0\le t\le z,
    \end{cases}\](so, with notation as in \cref{eq:phi} we have $\psi_z(t)=t\phi(z/t)$).
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Suppose $pn^{1/d_2(H)}\to c$ and $L/\mathbb EX_H(G)\to z$ as $n\to\infty$. Then, for $G\sim \mathbb G(n,p)$ we have
        \[\log \mathbb P[X_H(G)\le L]= -(\Psi_{\mathrm{Bin}}(H,c,z)+o(1))p\binom n2,
        \]
        where
        \[\Psi_{\mathrm{Bin}}(H,c,z)=\min_{W\in \mathcal W} \bigg(
        \int_{[0,1]^2}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(W(\vec x)\log W(\vec x)-W(\vec x)+1\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)\operatorname d\vec x+\frac{2c^{e(H)-1}}{|\operatorname{Aut}(H)|}\psi_z(t_H(W))\bigg),\]
    with $\mathcal W$ being the set of all measurable symmetric functions $W:[0,1]^2\to [0,1]$.
        \item Suppose $2mn^{1/d_2(H)-2}\to c$ and $L/\mathbb EX_H(G)\to z$ as $n\to\infty$. Then, for $G\sim \mathbb G(n,m)$ we have
        \[\log \mathbb P[X_H(G)\le L]= -(\Psi_{\mathrm{Unif}}(H,c,z)+o(1))m,
        \]
        where
        \[\Psi_{\mathrm{Unif}}(H,c,z)=\min_{W\in \tilde{\mathcal W}} \bigg(
        \int_{[0,1]^2}W(\vec x)\log W(\vec x)\operatorname d\vec x+\frac{2c^{e(H)-1}}{|\operatorname{Aut}(H)|}\psi_z(t_H(W))\bigg),\]
        with $\tilde{\mathcal W}$ being the set of all measurable symmetric functions $W:[0,1]^2\to [0,\infty)$ satisfying $\int_{[0,1]^2} W(\vec x)\operatorname d\vec x=1$.
    \end{enumerate}

    In \cite{JPPSold}, in addition to investigating $\mathbb P[G\text{ is triangle-free}]$, the authors were also interested in the conditional distribution of $G$ given that it is triangle-free. label: thm:STS
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:STS}
    Let $n$ be such that an order-$n$ Steiner triple system exists. The number of order-$n$ anti-Pasch Steiner triple systems is
    \[n^{n^2/6}\exp\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(-(9/24)n^2+o(n^2)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big).\]
    Equivalently, a uniformly random order-$n$ Steiner triple system is anti-Pasch with probability
    \[\exp\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(-(1/24)n^2+o(n^2)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big).\]
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Heuristic calculations suggest that the expected number of Pasch configurations in a random order-$n$ Steiner triple system is $(1/24)n^2+o(n^2)$, which would make \cref{thm:STS} a ``Poisson-type'' tail bound. It is known that this expected number is \emph{at least} $(1/24)n^2+o(n^2)$ (see \cite{Sim18}), but it is surprisingly difficult to prove the corresponding upper bound. Some general machinery to compute expected values of this type is currently work in progress by the first author with Lenka Kopfov\'a, Richard Montgomery and Kalina Petrova.

label: rem:high-girth
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:high-girth}
To elaborate on the more general conjecture of Glock--K\"uhn--Lo--Osthus mentioned above: recall that a Pasch configuration has 4 triples and only 6 vertices. In general, an \emph{Erd\H os $k$-configuration} has $k$ triples and only $k+2$ vertices. Without going into detail, it turns out that Erd\H os $k$-configurations in a Steiner triple system are in certain respects analogous to $k$-cycles in a graph, and it is of interest to understand Steiner triple systems with ``girth'' at least $g$ (i.e., having no Erd\H os $k$-configuration for $4\le k<g$). Glock--K\"uhn--Lo--Osthus had conjectured an asymptotic formula for the number $\operatorname{STS}_g(n)$ of order-$n$ Steiner triple systems with girth at least $g$, and Kwan, Sah, Sawhney and Simkin~\cite{KSSS24} managed to prove the corresponding lower bound (i.e., $\operatorname{STS}_g(n)$ is at least as large as conjectured). Using the ideas in this paper, we can obtain upper bounds on $\operatorname{STS}_g(n)$ in terms of certain analytic variational problems. We are unfortunately not able to solve these variational problems in general, but surprisingly it seems that for sufficiently large $g$ these variational problems yield upper bounds on $\operatorname{STS}_g(n)$ that are strictly weaker than conjectured. This was discovered by ChatGPT 6 Pro; it is related to the fact that the $3\times 3$ grid hypergraph does not have a certain ``positivity'' property~\cite{Sid22}, but is very numerous among Erd\H os $k$-configurations for large $k$. This observation does not disprove the Glock--K\"uhn--Lo--Osthus conjecture (as our methods do not provide a corresponding lower bound), but we view this as strong evidence that the Glock--K\"uhn--Lo--Osthus conjecture is false. We have decided not to investigate this further in the present paper. (We mention this not to claim any kind of credit, but just to share information that may be of interest to the reader).

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:latin}
    The number of order-$n$ Latin squares with property $N_2$ is
    \[n^{n^2}\exp\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(-(9/4)n^2+o(n^2)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big).\]

title: Remark
body_md: Answering a question of McKay and Wanless, it was proved by Kwan, Sah and Sawhney~\cite{KSS22} (see also \cite{MW99,KS18}) that the expected number of $2\times 2$ Latin subsquares in a random Latin square is $n^2/4+o(n^2)$, so \cref{thm:latin} is a ``Poisson-type'' tail bound.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: To explain the connection between \cref{thm:STS} and \cref{thm:latin}: a Latin square can be equivalently viewed as a set of $n^2$ triples in the 3-partite 3-uniform hypergraph $K_{n,n,n}^{(3)}$, such that no two triples share more than one vertex (the three parts correspond to the rows, columns and symbols in the usual definition of a Latin square). In this language, a $2\times 2$ Latin subsquare is the same thing as a Pasch configuration.

title: Remark
body_md: Although it is not very relevant for the present paper, we remark that a different approach that works for small $\gamma$ is implicit in the work of Jenssen--Perkins--Potukuchi--Simkin~\cite{JPPSnew,JPPSold}. Indeed, while they do not explicitly solve any variational problems, they obtain asymptotics for the lower-tail large deviation rate function under certain conditions, which means their methods can be interpreted as implicitly yielding solutions to our variational problems. Their approach, translated to our setting, is as follows. One can show that any minimising weighting $\vec q$ must be a stationary point of $F$. This yields an equation that a minimising $\vec q$ must satisfy, which can be interpreted as a fixed point equation for a certain operator (in statistical physics language, this operator can be interpreted as a \emph{belief propagation} operator for a certain ``hard-core model'' associated with $\mathcal H$). If $\gamma$ is sufficiently small (namely, if $\gamma$ is below a so-called \emph{Gibbs uniqueness threshold}), one can show that this operator is a contraction in a suitable norm, so there is a unique fixed point.

label: eq:book-degrees-1
title: Proof
body_md:
We may assume $C\ge 1$. We trivially have $\Delta_{r}(\mathcal{H})\le 1$, so $(\lambda,C;p)$-degree-boundedness implies that
\begin{align}
\Delta_{s}(\mathcal{H}) &\le  Cp^{s-r}\text{ for all }s\in\{1,\dots,r\},\label{eq:book-degrees-1}\\
\Delta_{s}(\mathcal{H}) & \le C\lambda p^{s-r}\text{ for }s\in\{2,\dots,r-1\},\label{eq:book-degrees-2}\\
\Gamma(\mathcal{H}) & \le C\lambda p^{1-r}.\label{eq:book-degrees-3}
\end{align}
Fix $a\le A$ and $k\in\{1,\dots,a(r-1)\}$. Say an 
``$(a;k)$-book'' is an $a$-book with exactly $k$ page vertices. 
We represent $(a;k)$-books in the form $(v,e_1,\dots,e_a)$, where $v$ is the spine and $e_1,\dots,e_a$ are the pages.

First, for a vertex $v\in V$, let $\mathcal{B}(v)$ be the set
of $(a;k)$-books with spine $v$ (so $|\operatorname{bk}^a_k(\mathcal H;v)|=|\mathcal{B}(v)|$). For each $(v,e_{1},\dots,e_{a})\in\mathcal{B}(v)$,
we define ``overlap statistics'' $\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a}$, as
follows. Let $\ell_{1}=1$, and for $i\in\{2,\dots,a\}$ let $\ell_{i}=|(e_{1}\cup\dots\cup e_{i-1})\cap e_{i}|\ge1$
be the number of vertices of $e_{i}$ which already appeared in previous
pages. So, $\ell_{1}+\dots+\ell_{a}=ar-k$. We use these statistics
to stratify $\mathcal{B}(v)$: for $\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a}$
satisfying $\ell_{1}+\dots+\ell_{a}=ar-k$, let $\mathcal{B}(v;\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a})\subseteq\mathcal{B}(v)$
be the set of $(a;k)$-books with spine $v$ and these particular
overlap statistics $\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a}$. Then, using \cref{eq:book-degrees-1} we have
\begin{align}
|\mathcal{B}(v;\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a})| & \le\Delta_{1}(\mathcal{H})\cdot\binom{r}{\ell_{2}}\Delta_{\ell_{2}}(\mathcal{H})\cdot\binom{2r-\ell_{2}}{\ell_{3}}\Delta_{\ell_{3}}(\mathcal{H})\cdot\dots\cdot\binom{ar-\ell_{1}-\dots-\ell_{a-1}}{\ell_{a}}\Delta_{\ell_{a}}(\mathcal{H})\notag\\
 & \le O_{r,A}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(\Delta_{\ell_{1}}(\mathcal{H})\cdot\dots\cdot\Delta_{\ell_{a}}(\mathcal{H})\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)=O_{A,C,r}(p^{\ell_{1}-r}\cdot\dots\cdot p^{\ell_{a}-r})=O_{A,C,r}(p^{-k}).\label{eq:book-calculation-for-later}
\end{align}
Since there are at most $r^{a}\le O_{A,r}(1)$ choices for $\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a}$,
we deduce \cref{eq:book-degrees-goal-1}.

We can improve this bound if $k<a(r-1)$. Indeed, in this case, every $(a;k)$-book has a pair of pages that intersect in more than one vertex, so we can reorder its pages to make $\ell_2\in \{2,\dots,r-1\}$ (note that the pages of an $a$-book must be distinct, so we cannot have $\ell_2=r$). But if $\ell_2\in \{2,\dots,r-1\}$, we can use  \cref{eq:book-degrees-2} in place of \cref{eq:book-degrees-1} to bound $\Delta_{\ell_2}(\mathcal H)$, which gives
\[
|\mathcal{B}(v;\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a})| \le O_{A,C,r}(\lambda p^{-k}).\]
Since there are only $a!=O_A(1)$ ways to reorder the hyperedges of an $(a;k)$-book, we deduce \cref{eq:book-degrees-goal-2}.

Next, for fixed vertices $v_{1},\dots,v_{s}$, let $\mathcal{D}(v_{1},\dots,v_{s})$
be the set of $(a;k)$-books $(v,e_1,\dots,e_a)$ containing $v_{1},\dots,v_{s}$
among their page vertices, such that $e_{1}$ contains at least one
of these fixed vertices. So, $\operatorname{deg}_{\operatorname{bk}^a_k(\mathcal H)}(v_1,\dots,v_s)\le a|\mathcal{D}(v_{1},\dots,v_{s})|$.

For each $(v,e_{1},\dots,e_{a})\in\mathcal{D}(v_1,\dots,v_s)$,
we again define overlap statistics, though in a slightly different way: let $\ell_{1}=|\{v_{1},\dots,v_{s}\}\cap e_{1}\setminus v|\in \{1,\dots,r-1\}$
be the number of fixed vertices among the page vertices of $e_{1}$,
and for $i\in\{2,\dots,a\}$, let $\ell_{i}=|(\{v_{1},\dots,v_{s}\}\cup e_{1}\cup\dots\cup e_{i-1})\cap e_{i}|\ge1$
be the number of ``previous'' vertices among the vertices of $e_{i}$.
Then $\ell_{1}+\dots+\ell_{a}=s+ar-1-k$. For $\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a}$
satisfying $\ell_{1}+\dots+\ell_{a}=s+ar-1-k$, let $\mathcal{D}(v_{1},\dots,v_{s};\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a})\subseteq\mathcal{D}(v_{1},\dots,v_{s})$
be the set of $(a;k)$-books in $\mathcal{D}(v_{1},\dots,v_{s})$
with these particular overlap statistics $\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a}$. 

In general, using \cref{eq:book-degrees-1}, we have
\[
|\mathcal{D}(v_{1},\dots,v_{s};\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a})|\le O_{A,r}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(\Delta_{\ell_{1}}(\mathcal{H})\cdot\dots\cdot\Delta_{\ell_{a}}(\mathcal{H})\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)\le O_{A,C,r}(p^{\ell_{1}-r}\cdot\dots\cdot p^{\ell_{a}-r})=O_{A,C,r}(p^{s-k-1}),
\]
which already yields the desired bound $\Delta_{s}(\operatorname{bk}^a_k(\mathcal H))\le O_{A,C,r}(1)\cdot(\lambda^{1/(Ar)}p)^{s-1}\cdot p^{-k}$ in \cref{eq:book-degrees-goal-3},
in the case $s=1$.

It remains to establish \cref{eq:book-degrees-goal-3} in the case $s\ge 2$. For this, note that if any $\ell_i$ lies in the range $\{2,\dots,r-1\}$ we have the improved bound
\[|\mathcal{D}(v_{1},\dots,v_{s};\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{a})|\le O_{A,C,r}(\lambda p^{s-k-1})
\]
(using \cref{eq:book-degrees-2} in place of \cref{eq:book-degrees-1} to bound $\Delta_{\ell_i}(\mathcal H)$). Also, let $\mathcal D^*(v_1,\dots,v_s)\subseteq\mathcal D(v_1,\dots,v_s)$ be the set of $(a;k)$-books $(v,e_1,\dots,e_a)$ for which $e_1,e_2$ both contain exactly one of the fixed vertices $v_1,\dots,v_s$ (this implies $\ell_1=1$), and $\ell_2=r$. We have
\[|\mathcal D^*(v_1,\dots,v_s)|
\le O_{A,C,r}(\lambda p^{s-k-1})
\]
(stratifying according to $\ell_3,\dots,\ell_a$, and using the bound on $\Gamma(\mathcal H)$ in \cref{eq:book-degrees-3} to control the number of choices for $e_1,e_2$).

So, to prove the desired inequality $\Delta_{s}(\operatorname{bk}_k^a(\mathcal H))\le O_{A,C,r}(\lambda p^{s-k-1})\le O_{A,C,r}(1)\cdot(\lambda^{1/(Ar)}p)^{s-1}\cdot p^{-k}$, it suffices to show that for every $(a;k)$-book $(v,e_1,\dots,e_a)\in \mathcal{D}(v_{1},\dots,v_{s})$, there is a way to reorder the pages of our book to make some $\ell_i\in \{2,\dots,r-1\}$, or to make it lie in $\mathcal{D}^*(v_{1},\dots,v_{s})$.

To this end, first note that if there were a page containing more than one of the fixed vertices $v_1,\dots,v_s$, we could put it first to make $\ell_1\in \{2,\dots,r-1\}$. So, suppose that every page contains at most one fixed vertex, and reorder the pages so that $e_1$ and $e_2$ contain different fixed vertices. The only way we could fail to have $\ell_{2}\in \{2,\dots,r-1\}$ is if $\ell_2=r$, in which case our reordered $(a;k)$-book lies in $\mathcal{D}^*(v_{1},\dots,v_{s})$.

label: lem:harris
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:harris}
Fix a ground set $V$ and let $\mathcal D$ be a nontrivial ``decreasing property'': a nonempty family of subsets of $V$, closed under taking subsets. Let $Y$ be a sample from $\operatorname{Bin}(V,p)$, conditioned on the event $\mathcal D$. Then for every $W\subseteq V$, each possible outcome $U$ of $Y\cap W$, and each $S\subseteq V\setminus W$, we have
\[\mathbb P[S\subseteq Y\,|\,Y\cap W=U]\le p^{|S|}.\]
In particular, for each $v\in V\setminus W$ we have 
\[\mathbb P[v\in Y\,|\,Y\cap W=U]\le p.\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal D_U$ be the collection of subsets $Z\subseteq V\setminus W$ such that $Z\cup U\in \mathcal D$, and let $R\sim \operatorname{Bin}(V\setminus W,p)$. This is a decreasing property on $V\setminus W$. Then
\[\mathbb P[S\subseteq Y\,|\,Y\cap W=U]=\mathbb P[S\subseteq R\,|\,R\in \mathcal D_U]\le \mathbb P[S\subseteq R]=p^{|S|},\]
using Harris' inequality (see e.g.\ \cite[Theorem~4.2]{Gri18}).

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:seq-ent}
        Let $X\subseteq V$ be a random subset of a ground set $V$ (with any distribution). For a set $S\subseteq V$, let $\operatorname{ex}(S)\subseteq V$ be a set of ``possible extensions of $S$'', containing every $v\notin S$ for which there is an outcome of $X$ including $v\cup S$. (It may also include other $v$.)
        
        Let $T\in \mathbb N$. Independently from $X$, consider a uniformly random partition of $V$ into $T$ sets $V_1,\dots,V_T$ (i.e., each element of $V$ is allocated to an independent uniformly random part). Let $X_t=X\cap V_t$ and $X_{<t}=X_1\cup \dots\cup X_{t-1}$ for each $t$. Then
\[\operatorname H[X]\le \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{v\in V} \mathbb P[v\in X]\Big(1-\log\mathbb P[v\in X]+\log\mathbb P[v\in \operatorname{ex}(X_{<t})]\Big).\]
head: environment

label: eq:entropy-setup
title: Proof
body_md:
First, by the chain rule (\cref{fact:entropy}) we have
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname H[X_1,\dots,X_T]=\operatorname H[X]+\operatorname H[X_1,\dots,X_T\,|\,X]=\operatorname H[X] + \mathbb E|X| \log T.\label{eq:entropy-setup}
    \end{equation}
    By the chain rule and subadditivity (\cref{fact:entropy}) we have
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname H[X_1,\dots,X_T] = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \operatorname H[X_{t}\,|\,X_{<t}]\le \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{v\in V}\operatorname H[\mathbbm{1}_{v\in X_t}\,|\,X_{<t}]. \label{eq:entropy-setup-2}
    \end{equation}
Now, note that $\operatorname H[\mathbbm{1}_{v\in X_t}\,|\,X_{<t}]=\mathbb E[h(Q_{v,t})]$, where we write $Q_{v,t}$ for the random variable $\mathbb E[\mathbbm{1}_{v\in X_t}\,|\,X_{<t}]$. We have $\mathbb E Q_{v,t}=\mathbb P[v\in X_t]=(1/T)\mathbb P[v\in X]$ and $\mathbb P[Q_{v,t}\ne 0]\le \mathbb P[v\in \operatorname{ex}(X_{<t})]$, so by the concavity of the binary entropy function $h$ we have
    \[
         \operatorname H[\mathbbm{1}_{v\in X_t}\,|\,X_{<t}]=\mathbb E[h(Q_{v,t})] \le \mathbb P[v\in\operatorname{ex}(X_{<t})]\,h\bigg(\frac{\mathbb P[v\in X]}{T\mathbb P[v\in\operatorname{ex}(X_{<t})]}\bigg). 
    \]
    Now, for any $0\le x\le y\le 1$ we have
    \[
        yh(x/y) = -x\log(x/y) - y(1-x/y)\log(1-x/y) \le - x\log (x/y) + x,
    \]
    (where we have used the elementary bound $-z\log z \le 1-z$, which holds for all $z\in [0,1]$). Applying this inequality with $x=\mathbb P[v\in X]/T$ and $y=\mathbb P[v\in \operatorname{ex}(X_{<t})]$ yields
\[
         \operatorname H[\mathbbm{1}_{v\in X_t}\,|\,X_{<t}]\le -\frac1T\mathbb P[v\in X]\Big(\log \mathbb P[v\in X]-\log T-\log\mathbb P[v\in \operatorname{ex}(X_{<t})]\Big)+\frac1T\mathbb P[v\in X]. 
    \]
    Substituting this into \cref{eq:entropy-setup,eq:entropy-setup-2} (and using that $\mathbb E|X|=\sum_{v\in V}\mathbb P[v\in X]$) yields the desired result.

title: Proof
body_md:
For odd $A$, we have
    \[\sum_{a=0}^A(-1)^a\frac{\mathbb E[D_v(D_v-1)\dots(D_v-a+1)\,|\,\mathcal F]}{a!}\le \mathbb P[D_v=0\,|\,\mathcal F]\le \sum_{a=0}^{A-1}(-1)^a\frac{\mathbb E[D_v(D_v-1)\dots(D_v-a+1)\,|\,\mathcal F]}{a!}\]
    by the Bonferroni inequalities (i.e., the fact that the inclusion-exclusion formula alternately undercounts and overcounts).
    Also, by Taylor's theorem we have
    \[\sum_{a=0}^A(-1)^a\frac{\mu_v^a}{a!}=\exp(-\mu_v)+O\bigg(\frac{\mu_v^{A+1}}{(A+1)!}\bigg).\]
    Combining these estimates yields
    \[\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big|\mathbb P[D_v=0\,|\,\mathcal F]-\exp(-\mu_v)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big|\le O_M\Bigg(\frac{M^A}{A!}+\sum_{a=1}^A\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big|\mathbb E[D_v(D_v-1)\dots (D_v-a+1)\,|\,\mathcal F] - \mu_{v}^a\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big|}{a!}\Bigg).\]
    Substituting the lemma assumption, summing over $V$, and averaging over $\mathcal F$, yields
    \[
            \mathbb E\Bigg[\sum_{v\in V} \mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big|\mathbb P[D_v=0\,|\,\mathcal F] - \exp(-\mu_{v})\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big| \Bigg] \le O_M\bigg(\frac{M^A}{A!}+e\gamma\bigg)|V|.
        \]
        The desired result follows, assuming $A$ is sufficiently large in terms of $\beta,M$ and $\gamma>0$ is sufficiently small in terms of $\beta$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Our goal is to prove that 
\[\log \mathbb P[|\mathcal H[R]|=0]\le -\min_{\vec q\in [0,p]^V}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,p)+\mathcal H(\vec q)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)+\varepsilon pN.\]
To this end we will first rewrite $\log \mathbb P[|\mathcal H[R]|=0]$ in entropic terms (i.e., in terms of the entropy of the conditional distribution of $R$ given $|\mathcal H[R]|=0$). We will then apply \cref{thm:KS} to see that our conditional distribution can be written as a mixture of measures that behave like product measures from the point of view of the book hypergraphs defined in \cref{def:books}. We then apply \cref{lem:seq-ent} to each of the measures in the mixture, using \cref{lem:moment} and degree-boundedness to estimate the relevant quantities.

In addition to the parameters $\lambda,\varepsilon$ in the statement of \cref{thm:main-upper}, the proof will involve additional parameters $T,A,\gamma,\xi,\alpha,\beta,\theta,C_0$, which should be chosen as follows. First, $\alpha,\beta$ need to be small, and $T$ needs to be large, in terms of $\varepsilon,C$. Then, $\gamma$ needs to be small, and $A$ needs to be large, in terms of $\beta,C$ (this dependence will come from \cref{lem:moment}). Then, $\xi$ needs to be small in terms of $A,r,\gamma,C$, and $C_0$ needs to be large in terms of $A,C,r$. Then, $\theta$ needs to be small in terms of $A,r,\alpha,\xi,C_0$ (this dependence will come from \cref{thm:KS}).
Finally, $\lambda$ needs to be small in terms of $A,C,r,\gamma,\varepsilon,\theta$.

\medskip \noindent\textit{Step 1: Reducing to an entropic problem.} Let $\mathcal D$ be the collection of independent sets of $\mathcal H$, and let $Y$ be a sample from the conditional distribution of $R\sim \operatorname{Bin}(V,p)$ given $R\in \mathcal D$. Let $\mathcal L(Y)$ be the law of $Y$. Then, we compute
\begin{align}
        \log \mathbb P[|\mathcal H[R]|=0]=\log \mathbb P[R \in \mathcal D] &= -\operatorname D_{\mathrm{KL}}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(\mathcal L(Y) \,\|\, \mathrm{Bin}(V,p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)\notag\\
        &=  \operatorname H[Y] + \mathbb E\log\Bigg(\prod_{v\in V} p^{\mathbbm{1}_{v\in Y}}(1-p)^{\mathbbm{1}_{v\notin Y}}\Bigg)\notag\\
        &=  \operatorname H[Y] + \sum_{v\in V} \Big(\mathbb P[v\in Y]\log p + \mathbb P[v\notin Y]\log(1-p)\Big).\label{eq:prob-entropy}
\end{align}
Apply \cref{thm:KS} (with $r_0=A(r-1)$ and our parameters $\alpha,\xi,C_0$) to obtain a set $W\subseteq V$, and for any possible outcome $U$ of $Y\cap W$ let
\[\operatorname H^{U}[Y]=\operatorname H[Y\,|\,Y\cap W=U],\quad q_v^U=\mathbb P[v\in Y\,|\,Y\cap W=U].\]
Using this notation, we can break down the formula in \cref{eq:prob-entropy} over outcomes of $Y\cap W$, to get
\begin{align}
\log \mathbb P[|\mathcal H[R]|=0]&= -\operatorname D_{\mathrm{KL}}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(\mathcal L(Y\cap W) \,\|\, \mathrm{Bin}(W,p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big) \notag\\
&\qquad\qquad + \operatorname H[Y\,|\,Y\cap W]+\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \Big(\mathbb P[v\in Y]\log p + \mathbb P[v\notin Y]\log(1-p)\Big)\notag\\
& \le \mathbb E\Bigg[ \operatorname H^{Y\cap W}[Y] +\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \Big(q^{Y\cap W}_v\log p + (1-q^{Y\cap W}_v)\log(1-p)\Big)\Bigg].\label{eq:average-entropy-independent}
\end{align}
So, in order to obtain our desired upper bound on $\log \mathbb P[|\mathcal H[R]|=0]$, it suffices to prove a suitable upper bound, on average, on the quantities $\operatorname H^{U}[Y]+\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q^{U}_v\log p + (1-q^{U}_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)$.

\medskip \noindent\textit{Step 2: Sequential entropy.}
Fix any outcome $U$ of $Y\cap W$; we will next apply \cref{lem:seq-ent} (with the ground set $V\setminus W$) to obtain a bound on $\operatorname H^{U}[Y]$. Let $X$ have the conditional distribution of $Y\setminus W$ given $Y\cap W=U$, so $\operatorname H^{U}[Y]=\operatorname H[X]$. Let $q_v=q^U_v=\mathbb P[v\in X]$. The conclusion of \cref{thm:KS} tells us that, on average, the distribution of $X$ behaves like a product measure, from the point of view of our book hypergraphs.

For $S\subseteq V\setminus W$ and $v\in V\setminus W$, let $D_v(S)$ be the number of hyperedges $e\in \mathcal H$ such that $v\in e$ and $e\setminus v\subseteq S$. In other words, when $v\notin S$, this parameter $D_v(S)$ is (a lower bound on) the number of new hyperedges that would be introduced if we were to augment the induced subgraph $\mathcal H[S]$ with the additional vertex $v$. Let $\operatorname{ex}(S)$ be the set of $v\in V\setminus W$ such that $D_v(S)=0$, let $V_1\cup\dots\cup V_T$ be a uniformly random partition of $V\setminus W$, let $X_t=X\cap V_t$ and let $b_v(t)=b_v^U(t)=\mathbb P[v\in \operatorname{ex}(X_{<t})]=\mathbb P[D_v(X_{<t})=0]$. By \cref{lem:seq-ent}, we have
\begin{equation}
    \operatorname H[X]\le \frac 1T\sum_{t =1}^{T}\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}q_v\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(1-\log q_v+\log b_v(t)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big).\label{eq:seq-ent-application}
\end{equation} 
Now, 
let \[\mu_v(t)=\mu_v^U(t)=\Big(\frac{t-1}T\Big)^{r-1}\sum_{\substack{e\in \mathcal H[V\setminus W]:\\v\in e}}\;\prod_{u\in e\setminus v}q_{u},\qquad \tilde b_v(t)=\tilde b_v^U(t)=\exp(-\mu_v(t)).\]
That is to say, if we assume that $X$ is approximately a product measure, then $\mu_v(t)$ is an estimate for the expected value of $D_v(X_{<t})$, and $\tilde b_v(t)$ is a Poisson-type estimate for $b_v(t)=\mathbb P[D_v(X_{<t})=0]$.

\medskip \noindent\textit{Step 3: Elementary estimates.} Now, recalling \cref{eq:average-entropy-independent}, the next step is to use \cref{eq:seq-ent-application} to estimate $\operatorname H^U[Y] +\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q^{U}_v\log p + (1-q^{U}_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)=\operatorname H[X]+\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q_v\log p + (1-q_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)$. We will end up with an error term depending on the quantities $|b_v(t)-\tilde b_v(t)|$ (i.e., depending on the quality of our Poisson-type estimate, which depends on the extent to which $X$ is approximately a product measure). Afterwards, the last step will be to use the conclusion of \cref{thm:KS} together with \cref{lem:moment} to show that quantities of the form $|b_v(t)-\tilde b_v(t)|$ are small, on average.

Note that $q_v\le p$ for each $v$, by Harris' inequality (\cref{lem:harris}), so
\begin{equation}
    \mu_v(t)\le \sum_{\substack{e\in \mathcal H[V\setminus W]:\\v\in e}}\;\prod_{u\in e\setminus v}q_u\le p^{r-1}\Delta_1(\mathcal H)\le C\label{eq:nondegenerate-probability-pre}
\end{equation} using our assumption that $\mathcal H$ is $(\lambda,C;p)$-degree-bounded.

If $b_v(t)\le \tilde b_v(t)$ then $\log b_v(t)-\log \tilde b_v(t)\le 0$. Otherwise, $\log b_v(t)-\log \tilde b_v(t)\le (b_v(t)-\tilde b_v(t))/\tilde b_v(t)\le O_C(b_v(t)-\tilde b_v(t))$ (here we are using \cref{eq:nondegenerate-probability-pre} to see that $\tilde b_v(t)=\exp(-\mu_v(t))=\Omega_C(1)$, and we are using $\operatorname d\log x/\operatorname dx=1/x\le 1/\tilde b_v(t)$ for $x\in [\tilde b_v(t),b_v(t)]$). In either case, we have
\[\log b_v(t)-\log \tilde b_v(t)\le O_C(|b_v(t)-\tilde b_v(t)|).\]
Recalling \cref{eq:seq-ent-application}, for each $U\subseteq W$ we obtain
\begin{align}&\operatorname H[X] +\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q_v\log p + (1-q_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)\notag\\
&\qquad\qquad\le \sum_{v\in V\setminus W}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q_v-q_v\log q_v+q_v\log p+(1-q_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big) \notag\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad +\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} q_v \log \tilde b_v(t)
+ O_C\Bigg(\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^Tp\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}|b_v(t)-\tilde b_v(t)|\Bigg).\label{eq:H-expansion-independent}
\end{align}

Now, let $q_v=0$ for $v\in W$, and let $\vec q=(q_v)_{v\in V}\in [0,p]^V$. Using the elementary inequalities $q\le -(1-q)\log(1-q)+O(q^2)$ and $\log(1/(1-p))=O(p)$ we have
\begin{align}&\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q_v-q_v\log q_v+q_v\log p+(1-q_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)\notag\\
&\qquad \le -\sum_{v\in V}\bigg(q_v\log \frac{q_v}p+(1-q_v)\log \frac{1-q_v}{1-p}\bigg)+\sum_{v\in W}(1-q_v)\log \frac{1-q_v}{1-p}+O(p^2 N)\notag\\
&\qquad \le -\operatorname D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec q\,\|\,p)+O(p^2 N)+O(p|W|)\le -\operatorname D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec q\,\|\,p)+(\varepsilon/4)pN,\label{eq:H-KL-independent}\end{align}
using that $\alpha,\lambda$ are small with respect to $\varepsilon$ (recall $|W|\le \alpha N$ and $p\le \lambda$).
Also, with a Riemann sum approximation we have
\begin{align}\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} q_v \log \tilde b_v(t)&=-\frac 1T\sum_{t=1}^T\bigg(\frac{t-1}{T}\bigg)^{r-1}\cdot \sum_{v\in V}\sum_{\substack{e\in \mathcal H:\\v\in e}}\,\prod_{u\in e}q_{u}\notag\\
&=-\bigg(\frac1r+o_{T\to \infty}(1)\bigg)\cdot r\sum_{e\in \mathcal H}\prod_{u\in e}q_u\notag\\
&=-\mathcal H(\vec q)+o_{T\to \infty}(p^r|\mathcal H|)\notag\\
&=-\mathcal H(\vec q)+o_{T\to \infty}(CpN)\notag\\
&\le -\mathcal H(\vec q)+(\varepsilon/4) pN.\label{eq:H-mean-independent}\end{align}
(Here we write $o_{T\to \infty}(1)$ for a term that can be made arbitrarily small by making $T$ large, we are using that $T$ is large in terms of $C,\varepsilon$, and we are using $(\lambda,C;p)$-degree-boundedness to see that $p^r|\mathcal H|\le N p^r \Delta_1(\mathcal H)\le CpN$.)

Substituting \cref{eq:H-KL-independent,eq:H-mean-independent} into \cref{eq:H-expansion-independent}, we deduce
\begin{align}&\operatorname H[X] +\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q_v\log p + (1-q_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)\notag\\
&\qquad \qquad \le -\min_{\vec q\in [0,p]^V}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,p)+\mathcal H(\vec q)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)+O_C\Bigg(\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^Tp\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}|b_v(t)-\tilde b_v(t)|\Bigg)+(\varepsilon/2)pN.\label{eq:conditional-with-random-error-independent}\end{align}


\medskip \noindent\textit{Step 4: Poisson approximation.}
Now, the final step is to use \cref{lem:moment} to show that the ``error term'' $\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}|b_v(t)-\tilde b_v(t)|$ is small, on average.

Let $\operatorname{bk}^a(\mathcal H[V\setminus W];v)=\bigcup_{k}\operatorname{bk}^a_k(\mathcal H[V\setminus W];v)$ and observe that these book hypergraphs were defined precisely so that
\begin{align}
\mathbb E[D_v(X_{<t})(D_v(X_{<t})-1)\dots(D_v(X_{<t})-a+1)]&=\sum_{e\in \operatorname{bk}^a(\mathcal H[V\setminus W];v)}\mathbb E[\mathbbm{1}_{e\subseteq X_{<t}}]\notag\\
&=\sum_{k=r-1}^{a(r-1)}\bigg(\frac{t-1}T\bigg)^k\sum_{e\in \operatorname{bk}^a_k(\mathcal H[V\setminus W];v)}\mathbb E[\mathbbm{1}_{e\subseteq X}].\label{eq:falling-factorial-independent}\end{align}
Also, recalling $q_u=\mathbb E[\mathbbm{1}_{u\in X}]$, and writing $q_e(t)=((t-1)/T)^{|e|}\prod_{u\in e}q_u$, we have
\begin{align*}&\sum_{k=r-1}^{a(r-1)}\bigg(\frac{t-1}T\bigg)^k\sum_{e\in \operatorname{bk}^a_k(\mathcal H[V\setminus W];v)}\;\prod_{u\in e}\mathbb E[\mathbbm{1}_{u\in  X}]\\
&\qquad =\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\sum_{e\owns v}q_{e\setminus v}(t)\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)^{a}\pm \sum_{\substack{e_{1},\dots,e_{a}\owns v\\\text{some }e_i=e_j}}q_{e_{1}\setminus v}(t)\dots  q_{e_{a}\setminus v}(t)\pm
 \sum_{\substack{e_{1},\dots,e_{a}\owns v\text{ distinct}\\|(e_1\cup \dots\cup e_a)\setminus v|<a(r-1)}}q_{(e_{1}\cup\dots\cup e_{a})\setminus v}(t),
\end{align*}
where the sums are over (sequences of) hyperedges in $\mathcal H[V\setminus W]$. Note that $\sum_{e\owns v}q_{e\setminus v}(t)=\mu_v(t)$ and
\[ \sum_{\substack{e_{1},\dots,e_{a}\owns v\text{ distinct}\\|(e_1\cup \dots\cup e_a)\setminus v|<a(r-1)}}q_{(e_{1}\cup\dots\cup e_{a})\setminus v}(t)\le \sum_{k=r-1}^{a(r-1)-1}p^{k}|\operatorname{bk}^a_k(\mathcal H;v)|=O_{A,C,r}(\lambda)\le \gamma/4\]
by \cref{eq:book-degrees-goal-2} in \cref{lem:book-deg} (using that $\lambda$ is small in terms of $A,C,r,\gamma$), and
\begin{align*}
\sum_{\substack{e_{1},\dots,e_{a}\owns v\\\text{some }e_i=e_j}}q_{e_{1}\setminus v}(t)\dots  q_{e_{a}\setminus v}(t)\le \binom a2\sum_{e\owns v}q_{e\setminus v}(t)^2\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\sum_{e\owns v}q_{e\setminus v}(t)\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)^{a-2}&\le  O_{A}\Big(\Delta_1(\mathcal H)p^{2(r-1)}(\Delta_1(\mathcal H)p^{r-1})^{a-2}\Big)\\&\le O_{A,C}(p^{r-1})\le O_{A,C}(\lambda)\le \gamma/4
\end{align*}
by $(\lambda,C;p)$-degree-boundedness, and the assumptions $p\le \lambda$ and $r\ge 2$. So, we have
\begin{equation}
   \sum_{k=r-1}^{a(r-1)}\bigg(\frac{t-1}T\bigg)^k\sum_{e\in \operatorname{bk}^a_k(\mathcal H[V\setminus W];v)}\prod_{u\in e}\mathbb E[\mathbbm{1}_{u\in  X}]=\mu_v(t)^a\pm \gamma/2. \label{eq:product-independent}
\end{equation}
Now, the conclusion of \cref{thm:KS} (recalling \cref{lem:book-deg} to verify the condition \cref{eq:KS-degree-condition}, using that $\lambda$ is small in terms of $\theta$) implies that 
\[
\mathbb E\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \Bigg|\sum_{e\in \operatorname{bk}^a_k(\mathcal H[V\setminus W];v)}\bigg(\mathbb E[\mathbbm{1}_{e\subseteq Y}\,|\,Y\cap W]-\prod_{u\in e}\mathbb E[\mathbbm{1}_{u\in Y}\,|\,Y\cap W]\bigg)\Bigg| 
\le  \xi N.
\]
Taking an appropriate weighted sum over $k$ then yields
\[
\mathbb E\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \Bigg|
\sum_{k=r-1}^{a(r-1)}\bigg(\frac{t-1}T\bigg)^k\sum_{e\in \operatorname{bk}^a_k(\mathcal H[V\setminus W];v)}\bigg(\mathbb E[\mathbbm{1}_{e\subseteq Y}\,|\,Y\cap W]-\prod_{u\in e}\mathbb E[\mathbbm{1}_{u\in Y}\,|\,Y\cap W]\bigg)\Bigg|
\le  a(r-1)\xi N
\]
which is at most $(\gamma/2)N$
(recalling that $\xi$ is small in terms of $\gamma,A$).
Then for all $t$ let $Y_t=(Y\setminus W)\cap V_t$ and $Y_{<t}=Y_1\cup \dots\cup Y_{t-1}$, so  $X_{<t}$ has the distribution of $Y_{<t}$ given $Y\cap W=U$. Substituting \cref{eq:falling-factorial-independent,eq:product-independent} into the above inequality, we obtain
\[
\mathbb E\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \Big|\mathbb E\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[D_v(Y_{<t})(D_v(Y_{<t})-1)\dots(D_v(Y_{<t})-a+1)\,\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big|\,Y\cap W\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big]-\mu_v^{Y\cap W}(t)^a\Big| \le  \gamma N,
\]
so, recalling \cref{eq:nondegenerate-probability-pre}, by \cref{lem:moment} (with $\mathcal F$ being the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $Y\cap W$) we have
\[
   \mathbb E\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}|b_v^{Y\cap W}(t)-\tilde b_v^{Y\cap W}(t)|=\mathbb E\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}\Big|\mathbb P[D_v(Y_{<t})=0\,|\,Y\cap W]-\exp(-\mu_v^{Y\cap W}(t))\Big|\le \beta N.
\]
The desired result then follows by combining this with \cref{eq:conditional-with-random-error-independent,eq:average-entropy-independent} (recalling that $\beta$ is small in terms of $\varepsilon,C$).

body_md:
\label{lem:moment-laplace}
        For $M, \beta>0$, there exist $A, \gamma>0$ such that the following holds. Let $\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra, let $(D_v)_{v\in V}$ be a collection of nonnegative integer valued random variables, and let $(\mu_v)_{v\in V}$ be a collection of $\mathcal F$-measurable random variables supported in $[0,M]$. Suppose that for all $a\in \{1,\dots,A\}$ we have
        \[
            \mathbb E\Bigg[\sum_{v\in V} \Big|\mathbb E[D_v(D_v-1)\dots (D_v-a+1)\,|\,\mathcal F] - \mu_{v}^a\Big| \Bigg]\le \gamma |V|. 
        \]
        Then, for any nonnegative $\mathcal F$-measurable random variable $\tau$,
        \[
            \mathbb E\Bigg[\sum_{v\in V} \Big|\mathbb E[\exp(-\tau D_v)\,|\,\mathcal F] - \exp(-(1-e^{-\tau})\mu_{v})\Big| \Bigg] \le \beta|V|. 
        \]

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\rho=1-e^{-\tau}$. We think of $D_v$ as being the size of a random set, and define $D_v'$ to be the size of a $\rho$-random subset of this random set. 
    Formally, conditionally on $\mathcal F$ and the random variables $(D_v)_{v\in V}$, we let $D_v'\sim \operatorname{Bin}(D_v,\rho)$.
    
    We compute
    \[ \mathbb P[D_v'=0\mid\mathcal F] = \mathbb E[(1-\rho)^{D_v}\,|\,\mathcal F] = \mathbb E[e^{-\tau D_v}\,|\,\mathcal F], \]
    and
    \[ \mathbb E[D_v'(D_v'-1)\dots(D_v'-a+1)\,|\,\mathcal F] = \rho^a\mathbb E[D_v(D_v-1)\dots(D_v-a+1)\,|\,\mathcal F].\]
    Since $0\le\rho \mu_v\le M$, the desired result then follows by applying \cref{lem:moment} to the variables $D_v'$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed in a similar way to the proof in \cref{subsec:independent-example}, so we will be brief with details that we have already seen there. We will need auxiliary parameters $T,A,\gamma,\xi,\alpha,\beta,\theta,C_0$, chosen in exactly the same order as in \cref{subsec:independent-example}.

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Step 1: Reducing to an entropic problem.}
The first step is basically the same as in \cref{subsec:independent-example}. Let $\mathcal D_{L,m}=\{S\subseteq V:|\mathcal H[S]|\le L\text{ and }|S|\le m\}$, and let $Y$ be a sample from the conditional distribution of $R\sim\operatorname{Bin}(V,p)$ given $R\in\mathcal D_{L,m}$. 
Apply \cref{thm:KS} with the parameters $r_0=A(r-1)$ and $\alpha,\xi,C_0$, to obtain a set $W\subseteq V$. For any possible outcome $U$ of $Y\cap W$ we let
\[\operatorname H^{U}[Y]=\operatorname H[Y\,|\,Y\cap W=U],\quad q_v^U=\mathbb P[v\in Y\,|\,Y\cap W=U],\]
and we obtain
\begin{align}
\log \mathbb P[|\mathcal H[R]|\le L\text{ and }|R|\le m]&= -\operatorname D_{\mathrm{KL}}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(\mathcal L(Y\cap W) \,\|\, \mathrm{Bin}(W,p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big) \notag\\
&\qquad\qquad + \operatorname H[Y\,|\,Y\cap W]+\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \Big(\mathbb P[v\in Y]\log p + \mathbb P[v\notin Y]\log(1-p)\Big)\notag\\
& \le \mathbb E\Bigg[ \operatorname H^{Y\cap W}[Y] +\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \Big(q^{Y\cap W}_v\log p + (1-q^{Y\cap W}_v)\log(1-p)\Big)\Bigg].\label{eq:average-entropy-lower-tail}
\end{align}

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 2: Tilted sequential entropy.}
As before, fix any outcome $U$ of $Y\cap W$, and let $X$ have the conditional distribution of $Y\setminus W$ given $Y\cap W=U$, so $\operatorname H^{U}[Y]=\operatorname H[X]$. Let $q_v=q^U_v=\mathbb P[v\in X]$. For $S\subseteq V\setminus W$ and $v\in V\setminus W$, let $D_v(S)$ be the number of hyperedges $e\in \mathcal H$ such that $v\in e$ and $e\setminus v\subseteq S$. Let $V_1\cup\dots\cup V_T$ be a uniformly random partition of $V\setminus W$, and let $X_t=X\cap V_t$.

We also need to make a new definition to incorporate the Laplace transform: let $d_{v,\tau}(t)=d_{v,\tau}^U(t)=\mathbb E\exp(-\tau D_v(X_{<t}))$.

By the definition of $X$ (via $Y$) we always have $|\mathcal H[X]|\le L$, so for any $\tau\ge 0$ we have $\operatorname H[X]\le\operatorname H[X]-\tau\mathbb E|\mathcal H[X]|+\tau L$. So, \cref{eq:seq-ent-tilted} gives
\begin{align}
    \operatorname H[X]\le\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}q_v\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(1-\log q_v+\log d_{v,\tau}(t)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)+\tau L.
    \label{eq:seq-ent-tilted-application}
\end{align}
Then, let \[\mu_v(t)=\mu_v^U(t)=\Big(\frac{t-1}T\Big)^{r-1}\sum_{\substack{e\in \mathcal H[V\setminus W]:\\v\in e}}\;\prod_{u\in e\setminus v}q_{u},\qquad \tilde d_{v,\tau}(t)=\tilde d_{v,\tau}^U(t)=\exp\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(-(1-e^{-\tau})\mu_v(t)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big).\]
\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 3: Elementary estimates and optimisation over the tilt.}
First note that 
$\mu_v(t)\le p^{r-1}\Delta_1(\mathcal H)\le C$
by $(\lambda,C;p)$-boundedness and Harris' inequality. So, $\tilde d_{v,\tau}(t)\ge e^{-C}=\Omega_C(1)$. As in \cref{subsec:independent-example}, considering separately the cases $d_{v,\tau}(t)\le \tilde d_{v,\tau}(t)$ and $d_{v,\tau}(t)> \tilde d_{v,\tau}(t)$, we see that
\[\log d_{v,\tau}(t)-\log\tilde d_{v,\tau}(t)\le O_C(|d_{v,\tau}(t)-\tilde d_{v,\tau}(t)|),\]
so we deduce from \cref{eq:seq-ent-tilted-application} that
\begin{align}&\operatorname H[X] +\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q_v\log p + (1-q_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)\notag\\
&\qquad\qquad\le \sum_{v\in V\setminus W}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q_v-q_v\log q_v+q_v\log p+(1-q_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big) \notag\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad +\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} q_v \log \tilde d_{v,\tau}(t)+\tau L
+ O_C\Bigg(\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^Tp\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}|d_{v,\tau}(t)-\tilde d_{v,\tau}(t)|\Bigg).\label{eq:H-expansion-lower-tail}
\end{align}
Let $q_v=0$ for $v\in W$, and let $\vec q=(q_v)_{v\in V}\in [0,p]^V$. Note that $\sum_v q_v\le \mathbb E |X|\le m$ by the definition of $X$ via $Y$. Exactly as in \cref{eq:H-KL-independent}, we have
\begin{align}&\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q_v-q_v\log q_v+q_v\log p+(1-q_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)\notag\\
&\qquad \le -\operatorname D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec q\,\|\,p)+O(p^2 N)+O(p|W|)\le -\operatorname D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec q\,\|\,p)+(\varepsilon/4)pN,\label{eq:H-KL-lower-tail}\end{align} and as in \cref{eq:H-mean-independent} we have
\begin{equation}\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} q_v \log \tilde d_{v,\tau}(t)\le -(1-e^{-\tau})\mathcal H(\vec q)+(\varepsilon/4) pN.\label{eq:H-mean-lower-tail}\end{equation}
Now, we set $\tau=\max(0,\log(\mathcal H(\vec q)/L))$, as the value\footnote{If $L=0$ we need to send $\tau\to \infty$, or in this case we can just use the $L=0$ approach in the previous subsection.} of $\tau\ge 0$ that minimises $-(1-e^{-\tau})\mathcal H(\vec q)+\tau L$, so that 
\[-(1-e^{-\tau})\mathcal H(\vec q)+\tau L=-\Phi_L(\mathcal H(\vec q))\]
(this is essentially just the Chernoff bound calculation for Poisson distributions). Combining this with \cref{eq:H-KL-lower-tail,eq:H-mean-lower-tail,eq:H-expansion-lower-tail}, we deduce
\begin{align}&\operatorname H[X] +\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(q_v\log p + (1-q_v)\log(1-p)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)\notag\\
&\qquad \qquad \le -\min_{\vec q}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,p)+\Phi_L(\mathcal H(\vec q))\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)+O_C\Bigg(\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^Tp\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}|d_{v,\tau}(t)-\tilde d_{v,\tau}(t)|\Bigg)+(\varepsilon/2)pN,\label{eq:conditional-with-random-error-lower-tail}\end{align}
where the minimum is over all $\vec q\in [0,p]^V$ whose sum of entries is at most $m$.

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 4: Poisson approximation for the exponential moments.}
It remains to control the final term in
\cref{eq:conditional-with-random-error-lower-tail}. We proceed in exactly the same way as in \cref{subsec:independent-example}, using \cref{lem:moment-laplace} instead of \cref{lem:moment}. Indeed, the calculations in \cref{subsec:independent-example} yield
\[
\mathbb E\sum_{v\in V\setminus W} \Big|\mathbb E\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[D_v(Y_{<t})(D_v(Y_{<t})-1)\dots(D_v(Y_{<t})-a+1)\,\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big|\,Y\cap W\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big]-\mu_v^{Y\cap W}(t)^a\Big| \le  \gamma N,
\]
so by \cref{lem:moment-laplace} we have
\[
   \mathbb E\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}|d_{v,\tau}^{Y\cap W}(t)-\tilde d_{v,\tau}^{Y\cap W}(t)|=\mathbb E\sum_{v\in V\setminus W}\Big|\mathbb E\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[\exp(-\tau D_v(Y_{<t}))\,\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big|\,Y\cap W\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big]-\exp(-(1-e^{-\tau})\mu_v^{Y\cap W}(t))\Big|\le \beta N.
\]
The desired result follows by combining this with \cref{eq:conditional-with-random-error-lower-tail,eq:average-entropy-lower-tail}.

title: Fact
body_md:
\label{fact:LO}
    Consider any $p\in [0,1]$ and $N\in\mathbb N_{\ge 0}$ such that $pN\in \mathbb N_{\ge 0}$, and let $B_{p,N}\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,p)$. Then $\mathbb P[B_{p,N}=pN]=\Omega(1/\sqrt{1+pN})$.

title: Proof
body_md:
First, note that for any $p\in (0,1)$ and $R_{p}\sim \operatorname{Bin}(V,p)$ we have
\[\mathbb P\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[|\mathcal H[R]|\le L]=\frac{\mathbb P\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[|\mathcal H[R_p]|\le L\text{ and }|R_p|=m\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big]}{\mathbb P\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[|R_p|=m\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big]}\le \frac{\mathbb P\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[|\mathcal{H}[R_p]|\le L\text{ and }|R_p|\le m\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big]}{\mathbb P\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[|R_p|=m\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big]}.\]
The key idea is to apply this inequality with $p$ much larger than $m/N$, so there is a huge entropy penalty for the event that $|R_p|$ is significantly less than $m$. This means that the conditional distribution of $R_p$ given $|R_p|\le m$ is very similar to the distribution of $R$.

The proof will involve an auxiliary parameter $B>0$, which must be large in terms of $\varepsilon,r,C$. We will take $\lambda$ to be small in terms of $B$.

\medskip
\noindent\textit{Step 1: Obtaining a clean variational problem.}
If $p=Bm/N$ then $\mathcal H$ is $(\lambda,O_{C,B,r,\varepsilon}(1);p)$-degree-bounded, so \cref{thm:main-upper-general} (with error parameter $\varepsilon/(4B)$) shows that
\[\log\mathbb P\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[|\mathcal{H}[R_p]|\le L\text{ and }|R_p|\le m\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big]\le -\min_{\vec{q}}\Big(\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,p)+\Phi_L(\mathcal H(\vec q))\Big)+(\varepsilon/4) m,\]
where the minimum is over all $\vec q\in [0,p]^V$ whose sum of entries $|\vec q|$ is at most $m$.

Then, letting $B_{m/N,N}\sim \operatorname{Bin}(N,m/N)$ and $a_B=\log B+\log(1-m/N)-\log(1-Bm/N)$, we compute
\[
\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,p)+\log\mathbb P\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[|R_p|=m\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big] 
  =\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,m/N)+a_B(m-|\vec{q}|)+\log \mathbb P[B_{m/N,N}=m].\]
  By \cref{fact:LO} we have $\log \mathbb P[B_{m/N,N}=m]\ge -O(\log m)\ge -(\varepsilon/4)m$ (using that $m\ge m_0$ is large).
So,
\[\log\mathbb P\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[|\mathcal{H}[R]|\le L\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big]\le-\min_{\vec{q}:|\vec{q}|\le m}I_B(\vec{q})+(\varepsilon/2)m,\]
where
\[
I_B(\vec{q})=\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,m/N)+\Phi_L(\mathcal{H}(\vec{q}))+a_B(m-|\vec{q}|).
\]
To prove the theorem, it suffices to show that
\[
\min_{\substack{\vec{q}\in[0,p]^{V}:|\vec{q}|\le m}
}I_B(\vec{q})\ge\min_{\vec{q}\in [0,1]^V:|\vec{q}|=m}I_B(\vec{q})-(\varepsilon/2)m.
\]

\medskip
\noindent\textit{Step 2: First reductions.}
Consider any $\vec{q}=(q_v)_{v\in V}\in[0,p]^{V}$ satisfying $|\vec{q}|\le m$;
it suffices to find $\vec{s}\in [0,1]^V$ satisfying $|\vec{s}|=m$ such that
$I_B(\vec{q})\ge I_B(\vec{s})-(\varepsilon/2)m$. There are two obvious candidates for $\vec s$: namely, the constant $(m/N)$-valued weighting $(m/N)\vec 1\in [0,p]^V$, and the rescaled weighting $\theta\vec{q}$, where $\theta=m/|\vec{q}|$.

So, suppose that the constant weighting $(m/N)\vec 1$ does not do the job: namely, suppose 
\[
  I_B(\vec{q})<I_B((m/N)\vec 1)-(\varepsilon/2)m<I_B((m/N)\vec 1)=\Phi_L(\mathcal H(m/N)).
  \]
  This implies that $L<\mathcal{H}(m/N)$ (otherwise we would have $\Phi_L(\mathcal H(m/N))=0$), and it implies that $I_B(\vec{q})\le \Phi_L(\mathcal{H}(m/N))\le \mathcal{H}(m/N)$. By $(\lambda,C;m/N)$-degree-boundedness we have $\mathcal{H}(m/N)\le O_C(m)$, so
  \begin{align}
      L&\le O_C(m),\label{eq:L-bound}\\
      I_B(\vec q)&\le O_C(m).\label{eq:I(q)-bound}
  \end{align}
Using that $I_B(\vec{q})\ge a_B(m-|\vec{q}|)=\Omega((m-|\vec q|)\log B)$ and $I_B(\vec{q})\ge \Phi_L(\mathcal H(\vec q))$, we deduce from \cref{eq:I(q)-bound} that
\begin{align}
m-|\vec{q}| &\le O_{C}(m/\log B),\label{eq:m-1}\\
\Phi_L(\mathcal{H}(\vec{q})) & \le O_{C}(m).\label{eq:m-2-pre}    
\end{align}
Then, we can use \cref{fact:Phi}(1) with \cref{eq:L-bound,eq:m-2-pre} to see that
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{H}(\vec{q}) \le O_{C}(m).\label{eq:m-2}\end{equation}

Now, our objective for the rest of the proof is to show that $I_B(\vec{q})\ge I_B(\theta \vec{q})-(\varepsilon/2)m$, using \cref{eq:m-1,eq:m-2}.

\medskip
\noindent\textit{Step 3: Continuity of $I_B$.}
By \cref{eq:m-1}, for each $v\in V$ we have $\theta q_v\le \theta p\le(1+O_{C}(1/\log B))\cdot B\cdot m/N$.
Writing $i_s(t)=t\log(t/s)+(1-t)\log((1-t)/(1-s))$, we compute
\[
    i_{s}'(t)=\log\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\frac{t(1-s)}{s(1-t)}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right),
\]
so, recalling that $m/N\le\lambda$, and $\lambda$ is small in terms of $B$, and $a_B=\log B+\log(1-m/N)-\log(1-Bm/N)$, we have
\begin{align*}
i_{m/N}(\theta q_{v})-i_{m/N}(q_{v}) &\le(\theta q_{v}-q_{v})\log\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\frac{\theta q_v(1-m/N)}{(m/N)(1-\theta q_v)}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)\\
& \le(\theta q_{v}-q_{v})(a_B+O(1/\log B+B\lambda)).
\end{align*}
Recalling that $\lambda$ is small in terms of $B,\varepsilon$, and $B$ is large in terms of $\varepsilon$, it follows that
\[
\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta \vec{q}\,\|\,m/N)-\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,m/N)\le(m-|\vec{q}|)a_B+(\varepsilon/4)m.
\]
Also, by \cref{eq:m-2,eq:m-1} and \cref{fact:Phi}(2), we have
\[
\Phi_L(\mathcal{H}(\theta \vec{q}))-\Phi_L(\mathcal{H}(\vec q))\le \mathcal{H}(\theta \vec{q})-\mathcal{H}(\vec{q})=(\theta^{r}-1)\mathcal{H}(\vec{q})\le O_{r}(1/\log B)\cdot O_{C}(m),
\]
so 
\[
I_B(\theta \vec{q})-I_B(\vec{q})\le (\varepsilon/4)m+O_{C,r}(m/\log B)\le(\varepsilon/2)m
\]
as desired.

label: rem:structure
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:structure}
The above proof shows how to study lower tail probabilities with respect to a random vertex subset constrained to have exactly $m$ vertices. It would be a simple matter to generalise this proof to allow for different constraints on the number of vertices in given sets (e.g., we could demand that in one vertex subset we take exactly $m_1$ vertices, and in a second vertex subset we take exactly $m_2$ vertices). By studying how such constraints affect the lower-tail probabilities, one can make conclusions about the typical structure of a sample from the unconstrained lower-tail event.

label: thm:GW-lower-bound
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:GW-lower-bound}
Fix constants $r\in \mathbb N_{\ge 2}$ and $Q\in \mathbb N$ and $C,\nu>0$. Consider a parameter $\alpha\in (N^{\nu-1},N^{-\nu})$, an $N$-vertex $r$-uniform hypergraph  $\mathcal G$, and uniform ``test hypergraphs'' $\mathcal F_1,\dots,\mathcal F_Q$ on the same vertex set $V$ as $\mathcal G$.
Suppose
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\mathcal G$ is $(N^{-\nu},C;\alpha)$-degree-bounded,
    \item Writing $k_i$ for the uniformity of $\mathcal F_i$, we have $k_i=O(1)$ and $|\mathcal F_i|\alpha^{k_i}\to \infty$, and $\Delta_s(\mathcal F_i)\le o(|\mathcal F_i|\alpha^{s})$ for $s\in \{1,\dots,k_i-1\}$.
    \item No hyperedge of any $\mathcal F_i$ contains a hyperedge of $\mathcal G$.
\end{itemize}
Then there is $m\in \mathbb N$ with $m=(1+o(1))\alpha N$, such that there are at least 
\[\binom{N}m\exp\Big(-\mathcal G(\alpha)-o(\alpha N)\Big)\]
size-$m$ sets $X\subseteq V$ satisfying $|\mathcal G[X]|=0$ and $|\mathcal F_i[X]|=(1+o(1))\alpha^{k_i}|\mathcal F_i|$ for each $i\in\{1,\dots,Q\}$.

label: thm:lower-bound-lower-tail-uniform
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:lower-bound-lower-tail-uniform}
In the setting of \cref{thm:GW-lower-bound}, for each $y\in [0,1]$ there is $m\in \mathbb N$ with $m=(1+o(1))\alpha N$, such that there are at least

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:prescribed-parts-lower}
For any $r\in \mathbb N_{\ge 2}$ and $\delta,C,\eta,\nu>0$, the following holds for sufficiently large $N$. Let $\alpha\in (N^{\nu-1},N^{-\nu})$ and let $\mathcal H$ be an $N$-vertex $(N^{-\nu},C;\alpha)$-degree-bounded $r$-uniform hypergraph. Let $\mathcal P$ be a partition of the vertex set into parts of size at least $\delta N$, and let $z\in [0,1]$.

Consider any $(m_W)_{W\in \mathcal P}\in \mathbb N_{\ge 0}^{\mathcal P}$ with $m_W\le (\alpha/2) |W|$ for each $W\in \mathcal P$, such that the sum of the $m_W$ is at least $\delta \alpha N$. Let $\vec x=(x_v)_{v\in V}\in [0,\alpha/2]^V$ be the vertex-weighting defined by $x_v=m_W/|W|$ for all $v\in W\in \mathcal P$. Then, there are at least
\[\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\prod_{W\in \mathcal P}\binom{|W|}{m_W}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)\exp\Big(-\phi(z)\mathcal H(\vec x)-\eta \alpha N\Big),\]
subsets $X\subseteq V$ satisfying $|\mathcal H[X]|\le z\mathcal H(\vec x)$ which have exactly $m_W$ vertices in each part $W\in \mathcal P$.

title: Proof
body_md:
In this proof we view $\delta,C,\nu$ as constants (i.e., when we write asymptotic notation, the implicit constants may depend on $\delta,C,\nu$).

    Consider some small $\varepsilon>0$ (we will need it to be small in terms of $\delta,C,r,\eta$), and
    for $W\in\mathcal P$ let
    \[u_W=\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\lfloor\frac{m_W}{\alpha}+\varepsilon|W|\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\rfloor\le |W|.\]
    Let $\mathcal U$ be the set of $U\subseteq V$ such that $|U\cap W|=u_W$ for all $W\in \mathcal P$. Using $(N^{-\nu},C;\alpha)$-degree-boundedness, we can compute that the average value of $\alpha^{r}|\mathcal H[U]|$, over all $U\in \mathcal U$, is $\mathcal H(\vec x)+O(\varepsilon\alpha N)=O(\alpha N)$, so by Markov's inequality there is a set $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{typ}}\subseteq \mathcal U$ with $|\mathcal U_{\mathrm{typ}}|\ge \Omega(\varepsilon)|\mathcal U|$ such that $\alpha^{r}|\mathcal H[U]|\le \mathcal H(\vec x)+O(\varepsilon\alpha N)$ for all $U\in \mathcal U_{\mathrm{typ}}$.
    
    Now, for all $U\in \mathcal U_{\mathrm{typ}}$, we apply either \cref{thm:GW-lower-bound} or \cref{thm:lower-bound-lower-tail-uniform} to $\mathcal H[U]$ (with adjusted values of $C,\nu$), with a 1-uniform test hypergraph for each part $W\in \mathcal P$. Specifically:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If $z>  2\varepsilon^{1/4}$ and $\mathcal H(\vec x)\ge  \varepsilon^{1/4}\alpha N$, apply \cref{thm:lower-bound-lower-tail-uniform} with $y=z-\varepsilon^{1/4}$. Note that if $S\subseteq U$ satisfies $|\mathcal H[S]|\le y\alpha^r|\mathcal H[U]|+o(\alpha N)$, then it satisfies $|\mathcal H[S]|\le y\mathcal H(\vec x)+O(\varepsilon\alpha N)\le z\mathcal H(\vec x)$ (for small $\varepsilon$). 
        \item If $z\le 2\varepsilon^{1/4}$ or $\mathcal H(\vec x)\le \varepsilon^{1/4}\alpha N$, apply \cref{thm:GW-lower-bound}, noting that an independent set $S\subseteq U$ certainly satisfies $|\mathcal H[S]|\le z\mathcal H(\vec x)$. In this case, set $y=0$, so $\phi(y)=1$.
    \end{itemize}
    In either case, we obtain some $m(U)=\alpha|U|+o(\alpha N)$ and some $(m_W(U))_{W\in \mathcal P}$ summing to $m(U)$ satisfying $m_W(U)=(1+o(1))\alpha|W\cap U|=(1+o(1))\alpha u_W$ (which in particular means $m_W(U)=m_W\pm 2\varepsilon \alpha N$ and $m_W(U)\ge m_W$) for all $W\in \mathcal P$, such that the number of subsets $S\subseteq U$ satisfying $|\mathcal H[S]|\le z\mathcal H(\vec x)$, with exactly $m_W(U)$ vertices in each part $W\in \mathcal P$, is at least
    \begin{equation}
        N^{-1/\delta}\binom {|U|}{m(U)}\exp(-\phi(y)\mathcal H[U](\alpha)-o(\alpha N))\ge \prod_{W\in \mathcal P}\binom{u_W}{m_W(U)}\exp\Big(-\phi(z)\mathcal H(\vec x)-(\eta/2)\alpha N\Big).\label{eq:lower-to-sum}
    \end{equation}
    Here we have used that $\phi$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, that $\varepsilon>0$ is small in terms of $\eta$, and that $\binom {n_1+\dots+n_J}{k_1+\dots+k_J}\ge \binom {n_1}{k_1}\cdot\dots \cdot\binom {n_J}{k_J}$. We have also used that $|\mathcal P|\le 1/\delta$, so there are at most $N^{1/\delta}$ possibilities of $(m_W(U))_{W\in \mathcal P}$ satisfying $m_W(U)=\alpha|W\cap U|+o(\alpha N)$ for each $W\in \mathcal P$.

    There are at most $N^{1/\delta}=\exp(o(\alpha N))$ possibilities for $(m_W(U))_{W\in \mathcal P}$, so there is $\mathcal U^*\subseteq \mathcal U_{\mathrm{typ}}$ with $|\mathcal U^*|\ge \exp(-o(\alpha N))|\mathcal U_{\mathrm{typ}}|\ge\exp(-o(\alpha N))|\mathcal U| $ such that $(m_W(U))_{W\in \mathcal P}$ takes a common value $\vec m^*=(m_W^*)_{W\in \mathcal P}$ for all $U\in \mathcal U^*$.
    Then, let $\mathcal T$ be the set of triples $(U,S,X)$ such that
    \begin{itemize}
    \item $U\in \mathcal U^*$,
    \item $X\subseteq S\subseteq U$,
    \item $|\mathcal H[S]|\le z\mathcal H(\vec x)$,
    \item $|U\cap W|=u_W$ and $|S\cap W|=m^*_W$ and $|X\cap W|=m_W$.
    \end{itemize}
    Summing \cref{eq:lower-to-sum} over all suitable $U$ and $S$, we have
        \begin{align*}|\mathcal T|&\ge\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\prod_{W\in \mathcal P}\binom{m_W^*}{m_W}\binom{u_W}{m_W^*}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)|\mathcal U^*|\exp\Big(-\phi(z)\mathcal H(\vec x)-(\eta/2)\alpha N\Big)\\
        &\ge \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\prod_{W\in \mathcal P}\binom{|W|}{u_W}\binom{m_W^*}{m_W}\binom{u_W}{m_W^*}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)\exp\Big(-\phi(z)\mathcal H(\vec x)-\eta\alpha N\Big).\end{align*}
    On the other hand, for any $X$ with $|X\cap W|=m_W$ for all $W\in \mathcal P$, the number of pairs $(U,S)$ for which $(U,S,X)\in \mathcal T$ is at most
    \[\prod_{W\in \mathcal P}\binom{|W|-m_W}{m^*_W-m_W}\binom{|W|-m^*_W}{u_W-m^*_W}.\]
    Using the identity
    \[\binom{u_W}{m^*_W}\binom{m^*_W}{m_W}\binom{|W|}{u_W}=\binom{|W|}{m_W}\binom{|W|-m_W}{m^*_W-m_W}\binom{|W|-m^*_W}{u_W-m^*_W},\]
we see that the number of $X$ which feature in some $(U,S,X)\in \mathcal T$ (which is a lower bound on our desired number of subsets) is at least
\[\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\prod_{W\in \mathcal P}\binom{|W|}{m_W}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)\exp\Big(-\phi(z)\mathcal H(\vec x)-\eta \alpha N\Big),\]
as desired.

Let $\eta>0$ be small (in terms of $A,C,r$), and let $\mathcal P^0$ be a partition of $V$ into (at most) $\lceil A/\eta\rceil+1$ parts, where we group vertices $v\in V$ according to which integer multiple of $\eta m/N$ is closest to $q_v$ (breaking ties arbitrarily). Letting $\delta=\eta^2/2$, there are at most $A\eta N$ vertices in parts of size less than $\delta N$. Let $\mathcal P$ be obtained by merging these vertices into a single part, and then merging this new part with some part of size at least $\delta N$. So, all parts of $\mathcal P$ have size at least $\delta N$, and the number of parts is at most $1/\delta$.

Let $\vec x^{\,0}=(x_v)_{v\in V}\in [0,Am/N]^V$ be obtained by averaging $q_v$ over each part $W\in \mathcal P$. By the choice of $\mathcal P$ (via $\mathcal P^0$) we have $\|\vec x^{\,0}-\vec q\|_1\le \eta m+(Am/N)(A\eta N)=O_A(\eta m)$. Let $\vec x$ be obtained by slightly altering the entries of $\vec x^{\,0}$ to ensure that the sum of the entries of $\vec x$ over each part $W\in \mathcal P$ is an integer $m_W\in \mathbb N_{\ge 0}$ (while still ensuring that the sum of $\vec x$ is exactly $m$, and that $\vec x$ is constant on every part). We can do this in such a way that $\|\vec x^{\,0}-\vec x\|_1\le 1/\delta$. By \cref{thm:prescribed-parts-lower} (with say $\alpha=3Am/N$, and adjusted values of $C,\nu$) we have
\[\log \mathbb P\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big[|\mathcal H[R]|\le L\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big]\ge\log\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\frac{\prod_{W\in \mathcal P}\binom{|W|}{m_W}}{\binom N m}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)-\Phi_L(\mathcal H (\vec x))
-\eta \alpha N.\]
Using \cref{fact:LO} (and using the notation therein), we compute
\begin{align*}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\frac{\prod_{W\in \mathcal P}\binom{|W|}{m_W}}{\binom N m}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)&=-\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{x}\,\|\,m/N)+\sum_{W\in\mathcal P}\log\mathbb P[B_{m_W/|W|,|W|}=m_W]-\log\mathbb P[B_{m/N,N}=m]\\
&=-\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{x}\,\|\,m/N)+O_\delta(\log N)=-\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{x}^{\,0}\,\|\,m/N)+O_\delta(\log N)\\
&\ge -\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{x}^{\,0}\,\|\,m/N)-(\varepsilon/2)m,\end{align*}
and by convexity we have $\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{x}^{\,0}\,\|\,m/N)\le \operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,m/N)$. body_md:
Let $X_{1},\dots,X_{n}$ be i.i.d.\ samples from the uniform
distribution on $[0,1]$.

For (1), we consider the \emph{random} weighting $\vec q=(q_{ij})_{ij\in K_n}\in \mathcal Q$ defined by $q_{ij}=pW(X_{i},X_{j})$. 
Using similar estimates as for \cref{lem:approximate-weighting-with-graphon}, we can compute
\[\mathbb E\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,p)=p\binom n2\int(W\log W-W+1)+o(pN)\]
and
\[\mathbb EX_H(\vec{q})=\mathbb EX_H(G)\cdot t_H(W)=p\binom n2\cdot \frac{2c^{e(H)-1}}{|\operatorname{Aut}(H)|}\cdot t_H(W)+o(pN).\]
We then observe that $\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,p)$ and $X_H(\vec{q})$ are both concentrated around their expected values: with probability $1-o(1)$ they both differ from their expected value by $o(pN)$. For example, one way to see this is using McDiarmid's bounded-difference inequality, noting that changing a single $X_i$ can affect $\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,p)$ and $X_H(\vec{q})$ by at most $O(np)$ (this uses that $p$ is in the critical regime, and $W\le 1$).

So, we can fix an outcome of $\vec q$ simultaneously satisfying $\operatorname{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\vec{q}\,\|\,p)=p\binom n2\int(W\log W-W+1)+o(pN)$ and $X_H(\vec{q})=\mathbb EX_H(G)\cdot t_H(W)+o(pN)$. The desired result then follows by the continuity of $\phi$.

For (2), we cannot \emph{a priori} assume that $W$ is bounded. Instead, we truncate $W$: define $W_{M}:[0,1]^{2}\to[0,M]$ by $W_{M}(\vec{x})=\min(M,W(\vec{x}))$.

We also need to make sure $\vec q$ is normalised appropriately. For this, it is convenient to introduce some notation. For a function $f:K_n\to \mathbb R$, we introduce the notation $\langle f\rangle =N^{-1}\sum_{ij\in K_n}f(ij)$. Let $w_0:[n]^2\to [0,M]$ be the random function defined by $w_0(i,j)=W_M(X_i,X_j)$ for $i\ne j$, and $w_0(i,i)=0$ for all $i$. Let $w_1=\langle w_0\rangle^{-1} w_0$ be a normalised version of $w_0$, and let $\vec q=(q_{ij})_{ij\in K_n}$ be defined by $q_{ij}=(m/N)w_1(i,j)$, so $\vec q$ has sum of entries exactly $m$.

Using a concentration argument as in (1), sending $n\to \infty$ for fixed $M$, we can prove that with probability $1-o(1)$ we have
\[\langle w_0\rangle=\int W_M+o_M(1),\quad \langle w_0\log w_0\rangle=\int W_M\log W_M+o_M(1)\]and, writing $\langle f(x_1,\dots,x_k)\rangle$ for the average of $f(x_1,\dots,x_k)$ over distinct $x_1,\dots,x_k\in [n]$,
\[\bigg\langle\prod_{ij\in H}w_0(x_i,x_j)\bigg\rangle = t_H(W_M)+o_M(1).\]
On the other hand, we have
\[\int W_{M}\to 1,\quad \int W_{M}\log W_M\to  \int W\log W,\quad t_H(W_M)\to t_H(W),\] as $M\to \infty$, by the dominated convergence theorem.
So, taking $M\to \infty$ very slowly as $n\to \infty$, we see that there is an outcome of $w_0$ satisfying
\[\langle w_0\rangle=1+o_W(1),\quad \langle w_1\log w_1\rangle=\langle w_0\rangle^{-1} \langle w_0\log w_0\rangle-\log\langle w_0\rangle=\int W_{M}\log W_M+o_W(1),\]
and
\[\bigg\langle\prod_{ij\in H}w_1(x_i,x_j)\bigg\rangle=\langle w_0\rangle^{-e(H)} \bigg\langle\prod_{ij\in H}w_0(x_i,x_j)\bigg\rangle=t_H(W)+o_W(1).\]
Then, it is not hard to see that the resulting weighting $\vec q$ satisfies the desired result.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $F(w_1,\dots,w_h)=(g(w_1)+\dots+g(w_h))/{h}+\gamma w_1\cdot \dots\cdot w_h$. Our task is to minimise $F(w_1,\dots,w_h)$ over all $w_1,\dots,w_h\in[0,1]$.
We will show that $F$ has a unique minimiser of the form $(w,\dots,w)$, which implies that the minimum value of $F$ is at least $\Psi_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{opt}}$.

First, we rule out minimisers on the boundary. If $w_i = 0$ then increasing $w_i$ by $\varepsilon$ decreases $g(w_i)$ by $\varepsilon\log (1/\varepsilon)+O(\varepsilon)$, while increasing $ w_1\cdot \dots\cdot w_h$ by $O(\varepsilon)$. Then, assuming each $w_j>0$: if $w_i=1$ then decreasing $w_i$ by $\varepsilon$ increases $g(w_i)$ by $O(\varepsilon^2)$ while decreasing $w_1\cdot \dots\cdot w_h$ by $\Omega(\varepsilon)$.

We deduce that every minimiser $(w_1,\dots,w_h)$ of $F$ lies in $(0,1)^h$ and is a stationary point of $F$, i.e., it satisfies 
\[\nabla F(w_1,\dots,w_h)=\bigg(\frac{\log w_i}h+\gamma \prod_{j\ne i}w_j\bigg)_{\!i}=\vec 0.\]

Now, fix a particular stationary point $(w_1^*,\dots,w_h^*)\in (0,1)^h$. We will show that if $(w_1^*,\dots,w_h^*)$ minimises $F$, then $w_1^*=\dots=w_h^*$. To this end, fix any two distinct indices $i,j$ and let $Q=h\gamma\prod_{\ell\notin\{i,j\}}w_\ell^*\le h\gamma\le e$ (using our assumption on $\gamma$). Stationarity tells us that
\[\log w_i^*=-Qw_j^*,\qquad \log w_j^*=-Qw_i^*.\]
Substituting these equations into each other, we see that both $w_i^*$ and $w_j^*$ are zeroes of the function 
\[f_Q(x)=\log x+Qe^{-Qx}.\]
Then, observe that for all $x>0$ we have \[f'_Q(x)=\frac{1-Q(Qx)e^{-Qx}}{x}\ge \frac{1-Q/e}{x}\ge 0,\] with equality only at $x=1/e$. That is to say, $f_Q$ is strictly increasing, so has at most one zero, meaning $w_i^*=w_j^*$. Since $i,j$ were arbitrary, this shows that $w_1^*=\dots=w_h^*$, as desired.

label: lem:EL
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:EL}
If $W$ is a minimiser of $\Psi_\gamma$ then for almost all $x,y$ we have
\[
   \log W(x,y)+\frac\gamma2\sum_{ab\in H} (R_{a,b}^W(x,y)+R_{b,a}^W(x,y))=0.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Delta_H W=\log W+(\gamma/2)\sum_{ab\in H} (R_{a,b}^W+R_{b,a}^W)$. Noting that $g'(w)=\log w$ and that $W$ is constrained to be symmetric, this is the functional derivative of $\Psi_\gamma$ at $W$; in other words, the first variation of $\Psi_\gamma(W)$ with respect to a symmetric perturbation $U:[0,1]^2\to \mathbb R$ is $\int (\Delta_H W)U$. For an interior minimiser $W$, the functional derivative $\Delta_H W$ must be zero almost everywhere, so to prove the desired result, we just need to rule out minimisers on the boundary.

To this end, first, note that if $W = 0$ on a set of positive measure, then increasing $W$ by $\varepsilon$ on this set decreases $g(W)$ by $\varepsilon\log (1/\varepsilon)+O(\varepsilon)$, while increasing $t_H(W)$ by $O(\varepsilon)$. So, for any $\Psi_\gamma$-minimiser $W$ we have $W>0$ almost everywhere. Second, if $W=1$ on a set of positive measure, then decreasing $W$ by $\varepsilon$ on this set increases $g(W)$ by $O(\varepsilon^2)$ while decreasing $t_H(W)$ by $\Omega(\varepsilon)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In this proof, asymptotic notation is as $\gamma\to \infty$. For a function $f:[0,1]\to \mathbb R$, we write ``$f=o(1)$'' to indicate that $\|f\|_1=o(1)$.

Let $W$ be a minimiser of $\Psi_\gamma$. By \cref{lem:weak-stability}, we have $\operatorname d_\square(W,G_k)=o(1)$. So, there is a realisation of the balanced complete $k$-partite graphon $G_k$ via some partition $I_1^0\cup \dots\cup I_k^0=[0,1]$ (where each $I_j^0$ has measure $1/k$) such that
\[\|W-G_k\|_1=\sum_{i,j}\Bigg|\int_{I_i^0\times I_j^0}(W(x,y)-G_k(x,y))\operatorname dx\operatorname dy\Bigg|=o(1).\]

We also record some further inequalities: by continuity of $g$ we have $\int g(W)=\int g(G_k)+o(1)=1/k+o(1)$, and by minimality of $W$ we have $\Psi_\gamma(W)\le \Psi_\gamma(G_k)$ so \begin{equation}
    \gamma t_H(W)=\Psi_\gamma(W)-\int g(W)\le \Psi_\gamma(G_k)-\frac1k+o(1)=o(1).\label{eq:small-hom}
\end{equation}

\medskip \noindent\textit{Step 1: Edge-criticality.}
We now explain how to use the edge-criticality of $H$. Since $H$ is edge-critical, there is an edge $ab\in H$ such that $H\setminus ab$ can be embedded in $G_k$ with $a,b$ in the same part $I_j^0$. So, for $x,y$ in the same part $I_j^0$, we have $R_{a,b}^{G_k}(x,y)=\Omega_H(1)$.

Since $\|W-G_k\|_1=o(1)$, we can obtain a similar conclusion with respect to $W$, as long as $x,y$ ``resemble two points in the same part of $G_k$''. Specifically, for any $x,y\in [0,1]$, if there is some $j$ and $\beta=\Omega_H(1)$ such that for all $\ell\ne j$ we have
\[\int_{I_\ell^0} \mathbbm{1}_{W(x,z)\ge \beta}\operatorname dz+\int_{I_\ell^0} \mathbbm{1}_{W(y,z)\ge \beta}\operatorname dz\ge 1/k+\Omega_H(1),\]
then for each $\ell\ne j$ there is significant overlap in the set of $z$ for which $W(x,z)$ is non-negligible and the set of $z$ for which $W(y,z)$ is non-negligible, and it is not hard to see that $R_{a,b}^{W}(x,y)=\Omega_H(1)$.
Recalling \cref{lem:EL}, we deduce that for such $x,y$ we have
\[
W(x,y)\le \exp\bigg(-\frac\gamma 2R_{a,b}^W(x,y)\bigg)=\exp(-\Omega_H(\gamma)).
\]

\medskip \noindent\textit{Step 2: Bounding the within-block densities.}
Since $\|W-G_k\|_1=o(1)$, 
there are ``typical'' sets $I_1^1\subseteq I_1^0,\dots,I_k^1\subseteq I_k^0$ of measure $1/k-o(1)$ such that 
\[
    W(x,\cdot)=G_k(x,\cdot)+o(1)\quad \text{for all }x\in I_j^1.
\]
By the considerations in Step 1, it is easy to see that $W(x,y)\le \exp(-\Omega_H(\gamma))$ when $x,y$ lie in the same typical set $I_j^1$. However, it is a bit more delicate to 
deal with the few exceptional $x$ which do not lie in any $I_j^1$. For this, we use a different type of local minimality property: minimality under the operation of ``removing vertices'' (in a certain continuum sense).

Specifically, letting say $\alpha_k=1/(10k)$ and $\beta_k=\alpha_k^2$, we claim that for almost all $x\in I_j^0$ we have
\begin{equation}
    \int_y \mathbbm{1}_{W(x,y)>\beta_k}\ge 1-1/k-\alpha_k.\label{eq:zykov-claim}
\end{equation}
To see this, suppose for the purpose of contradiction that there is a measure-$\varepsilon$ set $S\subseteq [0,1]$ such that \cref{eq:zykov-claim} fails for all $x\in S$. Then, let $W_{\bar S}$ be obtained by ``removing $S$ and rescaling the domain accordingly''\footnote{For almost all our different types of techniques to solve variational problems, throughout this section, it doesn't really make any difference whether we consider the ``discrete'' variational problems in \cref{thm:main-graphs} or their continuum variants in \cref{cor:main-graphs}. This rescaling argument seems to be the main exception (in the discrete world, the natural approach would be some kind of \emph{Zykov symmetrisation}, see e.g.\ \cite[Lemma~1.2.7]{Zha23}).}: for example, if (without loss of generality) we had $S=[1-\varepsilon,1]$, we would take
$W_{\bar S}(x,y)=W((1-\varepsilon)x,(1-\varepsilon)y)$. Now, for $x\in S$ we have $\int_y g(W(x,y))\ge (1/k+\alpha_k)g(\beta_k)\ge 1/k+\Omega_k(1)$, so $\int g(W_{\bar S})\le (1-\varepsilon)^{-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big(\int g(W)-2\varepsilon(1/k+\Omega_k(1))+O(\varepsilon^2)\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\mathopen{}\mathclose\big)=\int g(W)-\Omega_k(\varepsilon)$ for small $\varepsilon$. On the other hand, $\gamma t_H(W_{\bar S})\le (1-\varepsilon)^{-v(H)}\gamma t_H(W)=\gamma t_H(W)+o(\varepsilon)$ by \cref{eq:small-hom}. For small $\varepsilon$, we therefore have $\Psi_\gamma(W_{\bar S})<\Psi_\gamma(W)$, contradicting the minimality of $W$.

Now, say that a vertex is ``$j$-small'' if $\int_{I_j^1}\mathbbm{1}_{W(x,y)>\beta_k}\operatorname dy< \alpha_k$. So, \cref{eq:zykov-claim} implies that almost all $x$ are $j$-small for at most one $j$.

In fact, \cref{eq:zykov-claim} and the considerations in Step~1 together imply that almost every $x$ is $j$-small for \emph{exactly} one $j$. Indeed, if $x$ is non-$j$-small for every $j$ then for any typical $y\in I_1^1\cup\dots\cup I_k^1$ we have 
$W(x,y)\le \exp(-\Omega_H(\gamma))=o(1)$ for any typical $y$, by the considerations in Step~1. Recalling that all but an $o(1)$-fraction of $y$ are typical, this contradicts \cref{eq:zykov-claim}.

Now, let $I_j$ be the set of $x$ which are $j$-small. We have established that $I_1,\dots,I_k$ form a partition of $[0,1]$ (ignoring measure-zero sets). Note that $I_j^1\subseteq I_j$ for each $j$, so each $I_j$ has measure $1/k+o(1)$. By \cref{eq:zykov-claim}, for almost every $x\in I_j$ we have $\int_{I_\ell}\mathbbm{1}_{W(x,y)>\beta_k}\operatorname dy\ge 1/k-2\alpha_k-o(1)$ for all $\ell\ne j$.
By the considerations in Step~1 we deduce
\begin{equation}
    W(x,y)\le \exp\bigg(-\frac\gamma 2R_{a,b}^W(x,y)\bigg)=\exp(-\Omega_H(\gamma))\quad \text{for $x,y$ in the same part $I_j$}.\label{eq:within-part-bound}
\end{equation}
\medskip \noindent\textit{Step 3: Bounding the between-block densities.}
Recall that $H$ has chromatic number $k+1$. So, for any $x,y$ in different parts $I_i^0,I_j^0$, we have $R_{a,b}^{G_k}(x,y)=0$ for all $a,b\in \operatorname V(H)$. Correspondingly, using \cref{eq:within-part-bound}, for all $x,y$ in different parts $I_i,I_j$ we have $R_{a,b}^{W}(x,y)\le \exp(-\Omega_H(\gamma))$, so by \cref{lem:EL} we have
\[|\log W(x,y)|\le O_H(\exp(-\Omega_H(\gamma))),\]which implies that
\[W(x,y)\ge 1-\exp(-\Omega_H(\gamma)).\qedhere\]
